nameStory: The Unicorn Prominent gets its magical name from the caterpillar's distinctive horn-like projection that rises from its back like a mythical unicorn's horn. This prominent bump gives the larva an unmistakable silhouette that early naturalists couldn't help but compare to the legendary creature.
description: The Unicorn Prominent is a medium-sized moth with a wingspan of about 1 to 1.4 inches across. Adults have mottled brown and gray wings with intricate patterns that help them blend seamlessly into tree bark during their daytime rest. Like other prominent moths, they hold their wings in a tent-like position when at rest, and their fuzzy, robust bodies give them a somewhat chunky appearance compared to more delicate moth species.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive variegated pattern of browns, grays, and lighter patches that create an excellent tree bark camouflage - the wings often have a mottled, almost marbled appearance

idTips.label: Wing Position
idTips.description: When resting, the moth holds its wings in a distinctive triangular tent shape over its body, rather than spread flat like many other moths

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: The body feels sturdy and robust with dense, soft fur-like scales that give it a fuzzy texture - much chunkier than delicate moths like geometrids

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized with wings spanning roughly the width of a large bottle cap or small tea saucer when fully spread

idTips.label: Caterpillar Horn
idTips.description: If you find the caterpillar, look for the unmistakable horn-like projection rising from the back - it feels firm to the touch and points upward like a unicorn horn

habitat: Look for Unicorn Prominents in mixed deciduous forests and woodland edges throughout New England, especially areas with their host trees like birches, poplars, alders, and willows. They're particularly common in moist areas near streams or wetlands where these trees thrive, from sea level up into the mountains.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with caterpillars starting to appear on host tree leaves. Look for tiny larvae on young birch and poplar foliage.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time for adults, which are attracted to lights at night. Caterpillars are most visible and largest during mid to late summer, sporting their distinctive horns.
seasonality.fall: Late-season caterpillars finish feeding and pupate. Adults become scarce as they complete their single generation for the year.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as pupae in the soil or leaf litter. No active stages visible above ground during the cold months.

funFact: Scientists recently discovered this moth was misidentified for over 200 years - it was moved from the genus Schizura to Coelodasys in 2021 based on DNA analysis, meaning field guides printed before then have the wrong scientific name!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other prominent moths in the Notodontidae family, but the Unicorn Prominent's variegated wing pattern is more mottled and bark-like compared to the cleaner lines of similar species. Remember: if the caterpillar has that distinctive upright horn, you've found your unicorn!
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name recently changed from Schizura unicornis to Coelodasys unicornis in 2021, so older field guides and websites may still use the outdated name. This is a great example of how modern genetic techniques are helping scientists understand evolutionary relationships better than appearance alone.
compareHints: Since this is the only Coelodasys species in our region, compare it to other prominent moths in the Notodontidae family. The Unicorn Prominent's wing pattern is more heavily mottled and variegated than most relatives, giving it superior bark-mimicking camouflage. Its caterpillar's single prominent horn also distinguishes it from other prominent moth larvae which may have different arrangements of bumps or projections.
